pedagogy.summary:
- **Age:** 9–11 years

- **Topic:** Evidence supporting ideas (evaluating evidence)

- **Standards — UK (DfE Upper KS2 Working Scientifically):** the statutory programme requires pupils are taught to use "identifying scientific evidence that has been used to support or refute ideas or arguments" (verbatim). This is the child's move from generating their own evidence to critically EVALUATING evidence behind claims — including recognising that evidence can refute as well as support.

- **Standards — US (NGSS SEP 7 Engaging in Argument from Evidence, grades 3–5):** the progression requires students to "construct and/or support [curriculum wording omitted; reference 3-LS2-1, 4-LS1-1]", to "compare and refine arguments based on an evaluation of the evidence presented", and to "distinguish among facts, reasoned judgment based on research findings, and speculation." Evaluating the strength of evidence that supports or refutes an idea is the core of this practice.

- **Operational details:** Builds on presenting one's own findings with causal explanations and trust (prerequisite mt_nyPMkeHlVJ). The distinctive skills are: (1) identifying WHICH evidence bears on a claim (relevant vs irrelevant), (2) judging whether that evidence SUPPORTS or REFUTES the idea, and (3) evaluating the STRENGTH of the evidence (a large, repeated, controlled study vs a single anecdote). This is the argument-evaluation heart of the domain and the foundation for later distinguishing correlation from causation and systematic from random error. Feeds forward to KS3 formal error analysis and report-writing (dependents mt_3jmBpEepYX, and downstream mt_ThTbUuNb3p).

- **Checkpoint:** Tier B (transitional/early-formal). A learner who can identify the evidence relevant to a claim, decide whether it supports or refutes the claim, and give a reasoned judgement of how STRONG that evidence is has met the bar. Formal error typology comes at KS3 (mt_3jmBpEepYX).
bestPractices: Teach that evidence can REFUTE, not only support — give claims that the data actually contradicts, so pupils learn to follow the evidence against a prior idea rather than defending it.
Build an explicit strength ladder: anecdote / single reading < small controlled test < large, repeated, controlled study — and have pupils place evidence on it and justify the placement.
Separate relevance from strength: first ask 'does this evidence even bear on the claim?', then 'how strong is it?' — two distinct judgements pupils often merge.
Use paired competing claims with a shared evidence pool so pupils must decide which claim each piece supports or refutes — the essence of argument evaluation.
Model distinguishing fact from opinion/speculation (per NGSS SEP 7) using real-ish science claims, so 'evidence' isn't confused with assertion.
keyRepresentations: An evidence-strength ladder (anecdote → single test → repeated controlled study)
A supports / refutes / irrelevant sorting board for a given claim
A claim with competing evidence cards, each weighed
A fact vs reasoned-judgement vs speculation sorter
A 'which claim does the evidence better support?' balance scale
commonMisconceptions: Assuming evidence can only support (confirm) an idea, not refute it — and defending a prior belief against contrary data (confirmation bias).
Treating all evidence as equally strong — giving a single anecdote the same weight as a large repeated study.
Confusing relevance with strength, or counting irrelevant-but-vivid information as evidence.
Mistaking assertion or opinion for evidence (not distinguishing fact from speculation).
Believing more evidence always wins, regardless of its quality or whether it actually bears on the claim.

learn.summary: For ages 9–11: learning to evaluate the evidence behind scientific claims — deciding which evidence is relevant to a claim, whether it supports or refutes the claim, and how strong it is (a single anecdote vs a large, repeated, controlled study). Learners separate the CLAIM from the EVIDENCE, distinguish among facts, reasoned judgement based on research findings, and speculation, and learn that evidence can tip against a prior belief. The centrepiece activity is a weighing/sorting task with evidence cards; a role-play debate and sorting/ranking/competing-claims checks are retained as complementary approaches.

activities.title: Weigh the evidence on a claim-balance
feedback: If a learner piles up many weak cards to outweigh one strong study, point out that a large repeated controlled study carries more weight than several anecdotes combined — ask them to compare how each was gathered.
If a vivid but irrelevant fact is placed on the balance, ask: 'Does this actually bear on whether the claim is true?' Irrelevant cards should sit off the scale.
If a learner refuses to let evidence tip against a claim they liked, acknowledge the pull of a prior belief and ask them to follow the evidence rather than defend the idea.
Praise explicit justification of a card's strength by how it was gathered (controls, number of trials, comparison group), not by how interesting it sounds.
activities.rationale: Evaluating evidence is an active sorting-and-weighing task combining three distinct judgements — relevance, direction (support vs refute), and strength. Making the weighing concrete and manipulable may help learners separate these and experience strength (not vividness or quantity) deciding the outcome, including against a prior idea.
sourceClaims: DfE Upper KS2 Working Scientifically requires identifying scientific evidence that has been used to support or refute ideas or arguments.

NGSS SEP 7 at grades 3-5 requires supporting an argument with evidence, comparing and refining arguments by evaluating the evidence presented, and distinguishing among facts, reasoned judgement, and speculation.
learnerActions: Take a concrete claim, e.g. 'chewing gum improves memory' or 'this plant food makes seeds sprout faster', written at the top of a balance scale (drawn on paper or shown on screen).
Receive a deck of evidence cards: a friend's story (anecdote), a single quick test, a large repeated controlled study, and a couple of irrelevant-but-flashy facts.
Sort each card onto a 'supports / refutes / irrelevant' board, then place supporting and refuting cards on the balance so the scale tips for or against the claim.
Assign each card a strength and justify the placement using a strength ladder: anecdote / single reading < small controlled test < large, repeated, controlled study.
State a final judgement: which way does the evidence tip, and is it strong enough to accept, reject, or stay unsure about the claim?

OPTIONAL interactive version: drag cards onto the board and watch the scale physically tip, with each card's strength weighting the balance, irrelevant cards visibly doing nothing, and a filter that greys out non-evidence assertions.
activities.intendedInsight: In science it is the STRENGTH and RELEVANCE of evidence that decides an argument — not simply how many weak cards you pile on, nor how vivid the story is (although several strong, independent studies that agree do add weight). Sometimes the evidence tips the scale AGAINST the claim you started out believing.

activities.title: Debate the claim out loud
feedback: If a learner 'wins' by sounding more certain, redirect to the evidence: strength comes from the test design, not the loudness of the claim.
If a learner cannot counter a weak anecdote, prompt: 'What stronger test could settle this — what would you compare against?'
Reinforce when a learner concedes because the other side's evidence is genuinely stronger.
activities.rationale: Argument from evidence is inherently dialogic; rehearsing evaluation and counter-argument in live exchange exercises the practice of comparing and refining arguments. This complements the balance-board task by requiring spoken, responsive reasoning.
sourceClaims: NGSS SEP 7 at grades 3-5 requires supporting an argument with evidence, comparing and refining arguments by evaluating the evidence presented, and distinguishing among facts, reasoned judgement, and speculation.
learnerActions: Take a side in a spoken exchange where a partner (another learner, a teacher in role, or a scripted persona) advances a claim backed by weak evidence — e.g. a single anecdote.
Refute it with stronger evidence, naming why your evidence is stronger (controlled comparison, repeated trials).
Defend your own claim when the partner challenges it, and judge the quality of the evidence the partner offers rather than how confidently they speak.
Reach a reasoned position, revising it if the opponent's evidence turns out stronger.
activities.intendedInsight: Argument from evidence is a real exchange: you marshal evidence to support or refute, weigh an opponent's evidence by its design, and change your mind when the stronger evidence demands it.

activities.title: Sort, rank, and compare evidence across claims
feedback: If relevance and strength get merged, split the two questions explicitly: first 'does this bear on the claim?', then 'how strong is it?'
If an assertion is counted as evidence, ask what was actually observed or measured to back it up.
When ranking, ask the learner to name the feature (controls, sample size, repetition) that moved an item up the ladder.
If a learner labels a reasoned judgement from research findings as mere opinion, distinguish it: reasoned judgement rests on gathered findings, whereas speculation or opinion does not.
With competing claims, prompt the learner to show that one card can support one claim while being irrelevant to or refuting the other.
activities.rationale: Explicit categorisation, sequencing, three-way fact/reasoned-judgement/speculation discrimination, and competing-claim sorting give structured practice and a check on each judgement. These recognition/sorting tasks assess the component skills but do not by themselves elicit independent construction or spoken argument; pair them with the weighing and debate tasks so learners also build and voice arguments, not only classify given items.
sourceClaims: NGSS SEP 7 at grades 3-5 requires supporting an argument with evidence, comparing and refining arguments by evaluating the evidence presented, and distinguishing among facts, reasoned judgement, and speculation.
learnerActions: Categorise a set of evidence items for a given claim as supports / refutes / irrelevant.
Sequence several pieces of evidence from weakest to strongest and explain the ordering.
Given a mix of statements, sort them into three kinds — a fact/observation, a reasoned judgement based on research findings, and a speculation or bare opinion — and say how you can tell them apart.

Given two competing claims and a shared pool of evidence, decide for each piece which claim it supports, which it refutes, or whether it is irrelevant to both — then judge which claim the pool overall better supports.

As a quick warm-up, compare two short investigations and say whose evidence is stronger (controlled comparison with many trials vs a single uncontrolled observation); the full claim-vs-evidence reasoning is developed in the seed-sprouting check, so treat this as a brief classification, not a repeat of it.
activities.intendedInsight: Support-vs-refute, relevance, strength ranking, and telling facts from reasoned judgement and from speculation are separable judgements you can apply item by item — and the same evidence pool can bear differently on competing claims.

activities.title: Claim-versus-evidence check (seed sprouting)
feedback: If a learner says 'Aisha's is fine — her seed sprouted', ask what she compared against; with no no-food group, the sprouting could be coincidence.
If a learner treats the assertion itself as the evidence, split it explicitly into 'the claim' versus 'the observation that tests it' for each child.
If a learner judges by who sounds surer or by authority, point out that strength comes from the design (control, number of trials), not from the person or their confidence.

Full-credit response: separates claim from evidence, judges by controlled comparison and sample size, and explains when evidence supports or refutes — rating strength by structure, not agreement or confidence.
activities.rationale: A contrast between a single uncontrolled observation and a controlled, replicated comparison surfaces the key tell: whether a learner can say WHY one design makes evidence trustworthy and the other does not. The probing questions distinguish partial understanding ('more seeds', 'a fair test') from a full account of control and replication.
sourceClaims: DfE Upper KS2 Working Scientifically requires identifying scientific evidence that has been used to support or refute ideas or arguments.
learnerActions: Read two accounts: Aisha says 'It works — I used the plant food once and my seed sprouted.' Ben says 'I planted 20 seeds with the food and 20 without, same everything else, and the food ones sprouted two days sooner on average.'
Decide whose evidence is stronger and explain why in terms of test design.
For each child, state the difference between the CLAIM ('the food makes seeds sprout faster') and the EVIDENCE (what was observed and how it was gathered).

Answer probing follow-ups: What did Ben compare against that Aisha didn't, and why does that matter? Does Aisha's sprouted seed prove the food worked, or could something else explain it? If Ben's food-seeds and no-food-seeds had sprouted at the same time, would that support or refute the claim?
activities.intendedInsight: Evidence is judged by its structure — a controlled comparison with multiple trials — not by whether it agrees with the claim or by who sounds more confident. A single confirming observation is not proof.

constraints: Build on the prerequisite of presenting one's own findings with causal explanations; this topic moves from generating evidence to critically evaluating evidence behind claims.
Formal error typology (systematic vs random error) and formal report-writing come later (KS3); keep judgements here at reasoned strength-rating, not formal error analysis.
Teach that evidence can REFUTE as well as support — include claims the data actually contradicts so learners follow evidence against a prior idea rather than defend it.
Keep relevance and strength as two distinct judgements learners must make separately.
Keep the three-way distinction among facts, reasoned judgement based on research findings, and speculation; do not collapse reasoned judgement into mere opinion.

Sorting, ranking, and multiple-choice tasks assess and drill the component judgements but do not by themselves elicit independent construction or spoken argument; pair them with the weighing and debate tasks where learners build and voice evaluations.
A static strength-ladder reference chart is useful for support but does not let the learner actively sort and weigh competing evidence; use it alongside, not instead of, a manipulable task.

The optional screen version (dragging cards, a tipping scale, a non-evidence filter) is one way to make the weighing concrete; a paper balance with physical cards achieves the same purpose without any particular technology.
reviewNotes: This is an agent semantic rewrite of saved teaching research; sources were NOT re-fetched or re-verified. All activities are research-informed proposals, not validated interventions, and citations support general teaching principles, not that these specific activities were tested.
The second NGSS source (Appendix F) was marked verified:false in the source row; treat its claim as unconfirmed.

An earlier candidate had collapsed the NGSS three-way distinction (facts / reasoned judgement / speculation) into 'fact vs opinion' and had dropped the paired-competing-claims approach; both are confirmed present and consistent here (summary, activity 3, and constraints).

The original row rated a static image as unable to support sorting/weighing and 3D as 'not spatial'. These are catalog-fit judgements, not established pedagogical laws; softened to scoped affordance/limit statements. A fixed strength-ladder image can still teach as a reference even though it cannot be manipulated.
The example claim 'chewing gum improves memory' is a vehicle for evaluating evidence, not an endorsed scientific finding; present it as a claim to be weighed, not as fact.
Activity 3's quick investigation-comparison overlaps with the activity 4 seed diagnostic; it is retained but explicitly scoped as a brief warm-up so the two do not read as redundant.

Self-audit: the seed-sprouting diagnostic is internally consistent — Ben's design (controlled comparison, 20 vs 20, multiple trials) is correctly stronger than Aisha's single uncontrolled observation; retained as stated.

probeDeeper: What did Ben compare against that Aisha didn't? Why does that matter?
Aisha's seed sprouted — does that prove the food worked? What else could explain it?
If Ben's food-seeds and no-food-seeds had sprouted at the same time, would that support or refute the claim?
What's the difference between the claim and the evidence in each case?
assess.correctAnswer: Ben's evidence is much stronger: he used a controlled comparison with many seeds (a fair test with multiple trials and a group without the food), so the difference can be attributed to the plant food. Aisha's is weak — a single observation with nothing to compare against; her seed might have sprouted anyway. A strong response separates the CLAIM ('the food makes seeds sprout faster') from the EVIDENCE (what was actually observed and how it was gathered), and judges evidence by control and number of trials.

errorPatterns.pattern: Confirming instance = proof: 'Aisha's is fine — her seed sprouted, so the food works.'
errorPatterns.nextMove: Ask what Aisha compared against; with no no-food group, the sprouting could be coincidence.
errorPatterns.revealedBy: Accepts a single observation as sufficient evidence for the claim.

errorPatterns.pattern: Claim/evidence conflation: can't separate what is being claimed from what was actually observed.
errorPatterns.nextMove: Split explicitly into 'the claim' versus 'the observation that tests it' for each child.
errorPatterns.revealedBy: Treats the assertion itself as the evidence.

errorPatterns.pattern: Judges by confidence or authority, not design: believes whoever sounds more sure, or the adult/teacher.
errorPatterns.nextMove: Strength comes from the test design (control, number of trials), not from who says it or how confidently.
errorPatterns.revealedBy: Bases evidence strength on the person rather than the method.

responseLevels.gap: Treats a single confirming observation as proof, or judges strength by who sounds more confident.
responseLevels.full: Distinguishes claim from evidence, judges evidence by its design (controlled comparison and multiple trials versus a single uncontrolled observation), and explains when evidence supports or refutes an idea — rating strength by structure, not by agreement or confidence.
responseLevels.partial: Prefers Ben's evidence and mentions 'more seeds' or 'a fair test', but can't fully explain why control and multiple trials make evidence trustworthy, or doesn't separate claim from evidence.

assess.diagnosticPrompt: Two children argue about whether a plant food makes seeds sprout faster. Aisha says, 'It works — I used it once and my seed sprouted.' Ben says, 'I planted 20 seeds with the food and 20 without, same everything else, and the food ones sprouted two days sooner on average.' Whose evidence is stronger, and why? What's the difference between their claim and their evidence?
assess.whatMakesItDiscriminate: A child with the concept judges evidence by its structure (controls, sample size, comparison), not by whether it agrees with the claim. A child without it treats any confirming instance as proof, or rates the more confident speaker as more right. The tell is whether they can say WHY Ben's design makes his evidence trustworthy and Aisha's doesn't.
